title: Installation
description: Start here when you are setting up Indexly or enabling optional feature groups.

items.question: How do I install Indexly on Windows, macOS, or Linux?
items.answer: On Windows, the recommended product install path is `py -m pip install indexly`. On macOS and Linux, Homebrew is the most convenient product install path, while `python -m pip install indexly` remains a cross-platform fallback. If you are preparing a contributor workstation, use the maintained Windows or Linux environment setup guide instead of only installing the CLI. Always verify with `indexly --version` and `indexly --help` after installation.

items.question: Why does the terminal say `indexly` is not recognized after installation?
items.answer: That usually means the current terminal session does not yet see the Python or Homebrew scripts directory. Open a fresh terminal first. If it still fails, verify that the package is installed, then review the platform-specific setup notes for Windows Terminal or Linux shell initialization.

items.question: How do I prepare a contributor workstation on Linux?
items.answer: Use the maintained `dotfiles-linux` workflow from the dotfiles repository. The default Linux path is to copy the bundle to `~/dotfiles-linux`, run `./bootstrap.sh`, reload Bash, then use `show-help` and `idxdocs verify` to confirm the shell and Project-Indexly docs toolchain. On development machines, use `update-lp` after changing the repo bundle so the live `~/dotfiles-linux` profile is refreshed; use `update-profile` only when you need to relink an already-synced local bundle.

items.question: Why do some commands mention missing features such as analysis or document support?
items.answer: Indexly keeps the base install lightweight, so some commands depend on optional extras. Install only the pack you need, such as `indexly[analysis]`, `indexly[documents]`, `indexly[visualization]`, or `indexly[pdf_export]`. This avoids pulling in heavy dependencies when you only need the core search workflow.

title: Usage Basics
description: These answers help you choose the right command and get productive quickly.

items.question: What should I run first after installing Indexly?
items.answer: A practical first session is: check `indexly --help`, index a folder, run a simple search, then try one structured-data command. That sequence confirms the CLI is available, indexing works, and your environment is ready for the workflows you care about.

items.question: When should I use `analyze-file` instead of a format-specific command?
items.answer: Use `analyze-file` when you want Indexly to detect the best route automatically, especially for mixed structured formats or operational artifacts such as AutoDoctor JSON and SQLite outputs. Use `analyze-json`, `analyze-csv`, or `analyze-db` when you already know the file type and want a more direct route.

items.question: Does Indexly work offline?
items.answer: Yes. Indexly is designed for local-first workflows. Search, indexing, and most analysis operations run against local files and local SQLite state, so you can work without sending content to an external service.

title: Rename Automation
description: Choose and operate Indexly's on-demand and watch-folder renaming commands safely.

items.question: Should I use `rename-file` or `rename-watch`?
items.answer: Use `rename-file` for an on-demand file or folder that already exists, especially when you need optional database path sync or organizer handoff. Use `rename-watch` when files arrive over time and should pass through a repeatable JSON-defined pipeline with settling, filters, counters, quarantine, operator retry, and crash recovery.

items.question: How do I preview automatic renaming before any file moves?
items.answer: Create the starter configuration, validate it, and then run `indexly rename-watch --config "./rename-watch.json" --once --dry-run`. The preview freezes the initial file set, models counters and collisions, and does not move files or consume counter state.

items.question: What happens when Rename Watch cannot move or name a file?
items.answer: Rename Watch never overwrites an existing destination. Depending on the job configuration and failure type, it applies bounded retries, leaves the unchanged source in place, or moves it to a unique quarantine incident directory. `--status` reports durable active failures and their IDs; `--retry-failures` performs a guarded operator retry under the same watch-root lock.

items.question: Does Rename Watch index files or update database paths?
items.answer: No. `rename-watch` is a standalone filesystem rename pipeline. Use `indexly watch` when you want live indexing, or use `rename-file --update-db` for an on-demand rename that should also synchronize existing Indexly database paths.

items.question: How do I run Rename Watch continuously as a Windows service?
items.answer: Use the supported WinSW workflow with a dedicated Indexly environment, a separate `INDEXLY_HOME`, and `NT AUTHORITY\LocalService` for local folders. After installing the wrapper, always run `sc.exe qc IndexlyRenameWatch` before the first start and after an upgrade. It must report `NT AUTHORITY\LocalService`, not `LocalSystem`; the service guide includes the safe correction command and health checks.

items.question: Why does my Windows Rename Watch service exit with code 1067?
items.answer: First inspect the WinSW wrapper and child error logs. An access-denied message for `python.exe` means the service account can reach the wrapper but not the complete Python runtime. Stop the service, grant its identity read and execute access to both the versioned environment and its base Python installation, then repeat `--check-config` and `--once --dry-run` before starting it again. A dedicated runtime outside a personal user profile is the safer long-term layout.

title: File Locations
description: These paths matter when you need to inspect state files, logs, or runtime storage directly.

items.question: Where is the main Indexly database stored?
items.answer: Indexly stores its main SQLite database as `fts_index.db` inside its user-writable runtime base directory. By default that base is `%APPDATA%\\indexly` on Windows, `~/Library/Application Support/indexly` on macOS, and `$XDG_DATA_HOME/indexly` or `~/.local/share/indexly` on Linux. If `INDEXLY_HOME` is set, that override becomes the base directory instead.

items.question: Where are cache files stored?
items.answer: The primary search cache file is `search_cache.json` in the same runtime base directory as the database. Some command-specific caches can also live closer to the working data, such as organizer or lister cache files created under a local `.indexly` folder when those workflows are used.

items.question: Where do Indexly logs live?
items.answer: Core runtime logs are written under the runtime base directory in the `log/` folder. Organizer workflows can also write JSON logs to a custom `--log-dir`, which is useful when you want audit trails stored beside the files you are organizing.

title: Supported File Types
description: Use these answers to understand both search-oriented and analysis-oriented format support.

items.question: What file types can Indexly search or extract?
items.answer: Indexly supports a broad set of local file formats, including text files, Office documents, PDFs, spreadsheets, markdown, logs, and several image workflows when the matching extras are installed. Exact extraction depth depends on the file type and the optional dependency groups you have enabled.

items.question: Can Indexly analyze JSON, NDJSON, CSV, Excel, Parquet, and SQLite files?
items.answer: Yes. Indexly’s analysis stack supports common tabular and semi-structured formats such as CSV, JSON, NDJSON, Excel, Parquet, and SQLite. The generic `analyze-file` command is often the safest starting point when you are not fully sure which route will preserve the most meaning.

items.question: Are NDJSON logs first-class inputs in Indexly?
items.answer: Yes. NDJSON is the preferred structured logging format in current Indexly workflows and can be summarized through the analysis pipeline. This makes it a good fit for machine-generated event streams and operational logs that would be awkward to manage as plain text.

title: Troubleshooting
description: These are the fastest checks when behavior looks wrong or a command seems to stop short.

items.question: Why does Indexly search return no results?
items.answer: The most common causes are: indexing has not been run yet, the database is stale, the query is too narrow, or the file type was never extracted the way you expected. Re-index the relevant folder, retry with a simpler query, and run `indexly doctor` if the environment still feels inconsistent.

items.question: What should I do when JSON or NDJSON analysis fails because of encoding or file structure?
items.answer: First confirm the file encoding and whether the input is really standard JSON, NDJSON, or an application-specific report format. Files with a UTF-8 BOM, mixed records, or operational report structures often work better through `analyze-file` or a dedicated route such as `analyze-autodoctor`, because those paths can choose a better interpretation strategy than a strict JSON-first flow.

items.question: How do I handle database or schema warnings?
items.answer: Use `indexly doctor` to inspect the environment and database state. If the tool reports missing columns or schema drift, follow up with `indexly doctor --fix-db` after reviewing the message. That route is designed to surface problems before you try more invasive troubleshooting.

items.question: How do I recover search results removed with `clear-search`?
items.answer: `clear-search` removes rows from the local FTS5 search index only; it does not delete source files. To recover search results, re-run `indexly index` on the folder that contains the files. If you used `--all`, re-index every folder you expect to search. If cache invalidation failed, remove `search_cache.json` from the Indexly runtime directory so future searches rebuild fresh cache entries.

title: Performance Tips
description: Use these suggestions when data volume grows and you want Indexly to stay responsive.

items.question: How do I measure Indexly performance without changing the search database?
items.answer: Run `indexly perf --show`. For a non-WAL database it opens SQLite read-only, runs bounded local probes, and refreshes only the checksummed performance record. It refuses WAL mode before opening SQLite so a read-only connection cannot create or update shared-memory state; it never checkpoints WAL or changes journal mode. Use `indexly perf --read` to read the latest validated record without opening SQLite or writing files. Values are labelled Observed, Indexly-derived, or Theoretical and compare this installation with its own baseline; they are not a hardware benchmark or a direct comparison with another machine.

items.question: When can Indexly apply a performance action?
items.answer: Only action-specific evidence can qualify `planner-optimize` or `fts-merge`; database size, page count, and a generic performance grade are not enough. Both actions require measured canonical Indexly FTS5 readiness `1` (`match`). A legacy record missing the readiness metric returns `collect_evidence`; run a fresh `perf --show`. Unmeasured or budget-unavailable readiness returns `unavailable` without inferring schema damage. Measured readiness `0` for an actually inspected noncanonical, missing, drifted, external-content, malformed, unsupported, or uninspectable definition returns `repair_required` and routes to Doctor. Apply also requires a current report, exact database bindings, WAL refusal, free space, a writer reservation, a verified synchronized backup, and confirmation. The result omits the private identity salt and indexed paths or content.

items.question: What do performance action exit codes 2 and 3 mean?
items.answer: Exit `2` means no database mutation committed: preflight or backup failed, the action transaction rolled back, or follow-up failed after a `no_op`. If backup cleanup is incomplete, `indexly.performance-error/v1` reports `mutation_applied: false`, `backup_verified: false`, `cleanup_incomplete: true`, and only the unverified candidate filename. Inspect and remove that named candidate in the configured backup directory before retrying; do not use it for recovery. A rollback after verified backup creation instead uses `indexly.performance-action/v1`. Exit `3` means a mutation was applied but audit persistence or the post-action report failed; treat it as partial success and do not retry blindly.

items.question: Does a large database or an Elevated performance status mean the index is corrupt?
items.answer: No. Database size, document count, vocabulary size, and theoretical capacity values are not corruption findings. `Elevated` means repeated baseline-relative degradation was observed, while ungraded states such as `collecting_baseline` or `inconclusive` mean there is not enough comparable evidence. Review `indexly perf --show`; use the separate read-only `indexly doctor --full-integrity` check only when integrity is in question.

items.question: How can I keep indexing and analysis fast on large datasets?
items.answer: Scope the work intentionally. Index only the folders you actually need, apply ignore rules for generated or temporary files, and use file-type filters when your workflow targets a known subset. On the analysis side, prefer routes that stream or summarize instead of flattening everything into one big in-memory table.

items.question: What is the safest way to inspect large operational artifacts or mixed datasets?
items.answer: Start with the command that can make the best routing choice. For example, `analyze-file` is often better than forcing a JSON-only route when the input may actually be NDJSON, a report document, or an application-specific export. That keeps the analysis path closer to the file’s real structure and avoids unnecessary reshaping work.

items.question: How do I reduce repeat work during audits or organizer reviews?
items.answer: Keep your index and your organizer audit workflow separate, and let the generated logs or caches work for you instead of rescanning everything manually. When you revisit the same tree often, consistent log and cache placement can save a lot of time.
